\chapter{The Curled Row, and One Letter from the Lips}
\label{ch:retroflex-runway}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the four retroflex consonants and plain pa, and hear the curled row apart from the dental one.}

Retrieve the curled row and plain pa cold, together with two marks from two chapters back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ṭa]{\mr{ट} — the tongue curled back}

\label{lesson:MR-W07-tta}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{ta} with your tongue on your teeth. Now curl the tip up and back until it touches the ridge behind them, and say it again.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ट}
\end{quote}

That second sound is \textbf{\mr{ट}}, \emph{ṭa}. Marathi has a whole row of these \textbf{retroflex} letters, made with the tongue tip curled back, and they are genuinely different words from the dental row you already write: \textbf{\mr{त}} and \textbf{\mr{ट}} are not variants.

The shape is a hook that opens to the right and hangs from the headline. It is the sound in \emph{ṭebal}, the borrowed word for table, and it is why this book has been writing \emph{ṭ} with a dot under it in every romanization you have read.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\mr{ट}} twice, then trace \textbf{\mr{त}} once beside it. Say each one with the tongue in the right place. If they sound the same, the tongue has not moved.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Teeth or ridge for \textbf{\mr{ट}}? (\textbf{Ridge.})

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%9F-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari tta stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭha]{\mr{ठ} — the curl, with the breath let out}

\label{lesson:MR-W07-ttha}



\begin{quote}
The four-way pattern again: you have the plain one, so you can predict the next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ठ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ठ}} is \emph{ṭha}: \textbf{\mr{ट}} with the breath released. You have now seen this step three times — \textbf{\mr{क}}/\textbf{\mr{ख}}, \textbf{\mr{च}}/\textbf{\mr{छ}}, and here — which is the point. Devanagari is built so that hearing one pair teaches you to expect the rest.

The shape is a plain circle sitting under the headline. It is the roundest letter in the alphabet and the easiest of this chapter to draw.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{ठ}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{ट}} once from memory and check the hook did not close into a circle.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two is a full circle? (\textbf{\mr{ठ}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%A0-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari ttha stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḍa]{\mr{ड} — the curl, with the voice on}

\label{lesson:MR-W07-dda}



\begin{quote}
Fingers on the throat, tongue curled back. Say \emph{ṭa}, then switch the voice on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ड}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ड}} is \emph{ḍa}, the voiced member of the curled row — the same relationship \textbf{\mr{ग}} has to \textbf{\mr{क}}.

Marathi needs it for \emph{ḍoḷā}, \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{}, a word that also carries the retroflex \textbf{\mr{ळ}} you learned in the doorway chapters. Draw the top stroke, then the body that curves down and closes to the left under the headline.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{ड}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set it beside \textbf{\mr{ठ}}: one closes into a ring, the other does not.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word for a part of the face starts with \textbf{\mr{ड}}? (\emph{\textbf{ḍoḷā}} — eye.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%A1-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari dda stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṇa]{\mr{ण} — the nasal with the tongue curled back}

\label{lesson:MR-W07-nna}



\begin{quote}
Every row in this alphabet ends with its own nasal. The curled row is no exception.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ण}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ण}} is \emph{ṇa}: the tongue curled back, the air through the nose. Set it against \textbf{\mr{न}}, the dental nasal you learned in your first chapter, and the difference is the same one you made a moment ago for \emph{ta} and \emph{ṭa}.

This is the single most useful letter in this chapter. It ends every Marathi infinitive this book teaches — \emph{bolṇe}, \emph{khāṇe}, \emph{jāṇe}, \emph{sāṅgṇe} — so once it is yours, the shape of \textquotedblleft{}to do something\textquotedblright{} is readable.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{ण}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{न}} once beside it and say both aloud, curling the tongue only for the first.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter ends \emph{bolṇe} and \emph{khāṇe}? (\textbf{\mr{ण}}, with the \emph{e}-mark after it.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%A3-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari nna stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pa]{\mr{प} — the lips, with the voice off}

\label{lesson:MR-W07-pa}



\begin{quote}
Leave the tongue alone for this one. Close your lips, and let the voice stay off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{प}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{प}} is \emph{pa}, the voiceless partner of the \textbf{\mr{ब}} you already write. Same lips, same closure, voice switched off — the fourth time this book has used that one distinction to give you a letter.

It opens \emph{pāṇī}, \textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{pāhṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}, and it stands inside \emph{punhā}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}, in the goodbye you already say. The shape is \textbf{\mr{ब}} without the inner dot: left bowl, right stem, headline across.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{प}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set it beside \textbf{\mr{ब}}: the missing dot is the whole difference on the page.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Voice on or off for \textbf{\mr{प}}? (\textbf{Off.})

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%AA-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari pa stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
